annotations.text:
DECIDED 20 OCTOBER 2026

A, with B's quieter line, and Ready. One plain line under the house names the step the hub is on, sent by that step as it starts. A quieter line under it appears only where there is something to know: leave it plugged in, and that it restarts by itself. The first start never shows the slow sentence. And it ends on Ready, the house fully lit and where to go next, instead of a dark screen.

Every other start stays J. B's count and C's amounts are on the next page with their cases; C's amounts can still go under A's line later if a long step still feels stuck.

On building it: the Wi-Fi's name and password are different on every hub, so Ready names them on the screen itself (right-hand board, changed on the day it was picked), drawn from letters prepared as pictures, as the rest of the splash's words are.

WHY THIS EXISTS (20 OCTOBER 2026)

A NUC set up from the USB stick now shows Elyir's startup right after the maker's logo. On its first start it then shows the house breathing, with nothing else, for as long as the first start takes: copying itself onto the drive (minutes), restarting, unpacking what it came with, downloading the rest of the hub (a gigabyte or more), and starting the house for the first time. Watching it, it looks stuck.

The startup decided on 7 October (design/boot/, J) says no progress and no words but the name, and one sentence only if a start is slow. That was decided for an ordinary start, which is seconds to a minute. A first start is an install: it takes many minutes, it happens once, and somebody is watching it on purpose. These boards ask what the first start alone should say. Every other start stays J, exactly.

Monitor or wall, the splash draws in this 1440x900 space and is scaled to fit the screen, so a 1920x1080 monitor shows these boards at 1.2x.

TODAY

Two minutes in, the house breathes and nothing says what is happening (left). It can be copying gigabytes, downloading, or genuinely stuck, and the screen is the same in every case.

At three minutes the splash's one sentence comes up (right), because it was written for an ordinary start: "This is taking longer than usual. If it stays like this, unplug it for ten seconds and plug it back in." On a first start it always comes up, and it can come up in the middle of the copy onto the drive. Following its advice there interrupts the copy. Whatever is picked here, the first start must not show that sentence.

A: ONE LINE

One line under the house, in plain words, saying the step the hub is on right now. It changes when the step changes, and it is sent by the step itself, so it is never a guess on a timer. The steps on a NUC with an empty drive: Moving onto this computer's drive. Getting the hub ready. Downloading the rest of the hub. Starting the house for the first time.

The case for it: it is the smallest change to J. The house is still the picture, and the line is in the place and the size of the sentence J already allows. Where leaving it alone matters, the line says so.

The cost: a long step is still one unchanging line for several minutes, so a download that has stalled looks the same as one that is nearly finished.

B: THE LINE, AND WHICH STEP

A's line, with "Step 1 of 4" above it and a quieter line under it where there is something to know.

The case for it: a person can tell how far through they are, and that the restart after step one is part of the plan rather than a failure. That restart is the moment a first start most looks broken: the screen goes black and the name is written again.

The cost: the count differs from unit to unit. A hub that runs from its stick has no step one, a hub with no internet skips the download, and a wall that finds a hub has different steps altogether, so "of 4" has to be worked out on the unit at the start. And steps are not equal: step one can be ten minutes and step four ten seconds, so 3 of 4 does not mean three quarters done.

C: THE LINE, AND HOW FAR

A's line, with the amount under it, counting up: 3.2 of 9.0 GB copied, 640 MB of 1.4 GB.

The case for it: this is the closest to the ask, which was to know exactly what is happening behind the scenes. Numbers that move are the one sign that cannot be mistaken for a frozen screen, and they say how long is left without anybody having to guess a time.

The cost: it needs the most building. The copy and the download have to report their progress to the splash, and the splash has to draw numbers it cannot know in advance, which means either digits drawn as pictures or Plymouth's text drawing and a font in the boot image. And the steps that have no amount (getting ready, starting) fall back to A.

READY: WHERE TO GO NEXT (EVERY DIRECTION)

Today, when the hub answers, the splash plays its ending and the screen goes dark. On a NUC with a monitor that is the last thing anybody sees, and nothing on it says the hub is ready, or where to go now.

So whichever direction is picked, the first start ends on this: the house fully lit, and where to go next. On a cable it is the hub's web address (left). With no cable the hub offers a Wi-Fi of its own, and the screen gives its name and password (right). A hub that ships has them on its label too; a NUC somebody flashed from the USB stick has no label, so this screen is the only place to read them. After that the screen can go to sleep like any monitor.

It is shown only once, at the end of the first start. A wall does not need it, because its panel opens instead.

AND THE WHOLE STORY, FOR WHOEVER WANTS IT

The ask was to see exactly what is happening. The screen can't say that in plain words for everybody, but it can for one person. Pressing Esc on a keyboard plugged into the NUC switches the splash to the full log, with the first start's own lines in it, and Esc again switches back. That is Plymouth's own, it should already work today, and it needs nothing on the screen to advertise it.

WHICH ONE

Recommendation: A, with B's quieter line under it where there is something to know ("Leave it plugged in. It restarts by itself when this is done."). And Ready, in every case.

A says what is happening in the fewest words, and it is the smallest step away from J, which was chosen for being simple. B's count is true on one unit and wrong on the next, and it implies an evenness the steps do not have. C answers the ask most literally, and I would build it if the line alone still feels stuck when it is watched on the NUC. The amounts can be added under A later without changing anything else here.

Or something else: describe it, and I'll draw it.

WHY (20 OCTOBER 2026)

Ready, as built, names the hub's Wi-Fi and its password, and somebody types both into a phone. The question asked on the day: is this the moment to let the phone do it instead, with a code to scan?

It is. A phone's camera reads a Wi-Fi code and offers to join in one tap, on iPhone and Android alike, and the hub's Wi-Fi then sends the phone straight to setup. On a cable, the same code opens the hub's address. The name and password stay, smaller, for a phone that won't scan, which is also how somebody joins from a laptop.

The code is drawn on the unit, from that hub's own Wi-Fi, so it is never a picture prepared in advance. Dark on a light tile, because that is the way round every camera reads; a light code on the dark screen is not reliably read.

D: THE CODE BESIDE THE WORDS

The house stays exactly where every start leaves it, and the code and its words go under it, side by side.

The case for it: nothing moves. The startup ends the way it always ends, and Ready is added under the house.

The cost: the house holds the middle of the screen, so the code is small and pushed to the bottom edge, about 200 px on this space. Close up it scans; across a room it may not.

E: THE CODE IN THE MIDDLE

When the hub is ready, the house rises and gets small, and the code takes the middle of the screen, with the words under it.

The case for it: the code is the thing to do now, so it gets the place on the screen where the eye already is, at nearly half again D's size, which a phone reads from a chair. The house is still there, lit, saying whose screen this is.

The cost: one more motion at the end of the startup, the house moving up, which J does not have.

WHICH ONE

Recommendation: E. The whole point of this screen is the next step, and E gives the next step the middle of the screen at a size that scans from across a room. The house rising is one small motion, at the moment the startup is over anyway.

Or keep Ready as built, words only, or something else: describe it.

DECIDED 20 OCTOBER 2026

E. When the hub is ready the house rises and gets small, and a code to scan takes the middle of the screen, made on the unit from that hub's own Wi-Fi (or, on a cable, its address), with the name and password small under it for a phone that won't scan. It replaces the words-only Ready on the first page. D is on the next page with its case.

WHY THIS IS BACK (18 NOVEMBER 2026)

The first NUC set up from the stick sat on "Getting the hub ready" long enough that the person watching nearly gave up, sure it had frozen. "Nothing moves": the lamp does breathe, but from 72% to full over 6.4 seconds, which is too slow and too slight to read as life on a monitor across a desk.

The 20 October decision kept this open on purpose: "C's amounts can still go under A's line later if a long step still feels stuck." This is that day. The words chosen then stay; this page asks what moves, and how often the line changes, on a first start only. Every other start stays J, and a first start still never shows the slow sentence.

TODAY

On a NUC, "Getting the hub ready" is one line over three pieces of work: the system growing to fill its disk (seconds), loading the three containers the image carries off the USB stick (the brain, the front door and the broker, about 290 MB, so well under a minute on most sticks), and install.sh up to the point it starts the house. With no cable there is no download step, so the next thing it ever says is "Starting the house for the first time".

How long each part takes has not been measured on the NUC yet; its first-boot log will say. 290 MB doesn't explain minutes, so the long part is most likely inside install.sh with no network, where anything that reaches for the internet waits for its timeout. That is worth fixing on its own, whatever is picked here.

The two boards are two minutes and seven minutes in. They are the same picture, which is the problem.

A: NAMED STEPS

The same line, changed more often. "Getting the hub ready" becomes the steps it hides, each sent by the step itself as it starts, as today: "Unpacking what it came with" while the containers load, "Setting up the hub" for the install. And one quieter line under it, the whole way through: "A first start takes about 10 minutes. It happens only once."

The case for it: the smallest change. Two more step names in sequence.mjs, two more say.sh calls (firstboot.sh before docker load, install.sh at its start), and one more prepared line. The quiet line answers the real question, which is "is this normal?", before anybody asks it.

The cost: each step is still a still picture. If the install itself is the long part, that is still several minutes of one unchanging line. And "about 10 minutes" has to be true: it is a number measured on the NUC and the Pi, one per kind of unit, not a guess.

B: HOW FAR

A's steps, and where a step can be counted, a slim bar in the lamp's color and the amount under it, moving: the copy onto the drive in GB, the download in MB, the unpacking by bytes read. A step that can't be counted (setting up, starting) shows no bar and A's quiet line instead (B2), so nothing on the screen is ever made up.

The case for it: numbers that go up are the one sign nobody mistakes for a frozen screen, and unlike motion they stop when the work stops, so a stall looks like a stall. The splash can already draw it: digits come from the prepared letters Ready uses (GLYPHS), and the bar is one sprite scaled across.

The cost: the most building, and it lands on the steps that are long when they happen (the copy, gigabytes; the download, a gigabyte or more on a hub with a cable), not on the one that was watched, which can't be counted. The work has to report how far it is: the copy's dd checked against its size, docker compose pull read for progress instead of -q, and a small say.sh progress <done> <total> that sends elyir:p:<done>/<total> at most once a second.

C: VISIBLY ALIVE

A's steps, and motion that reads as working without measuring anything: on a first start the lamp pulses deeper and quicker (45% to full every 2.4 s instead of 72% every 6.4 s), a short light sweeps along a thin line under the words, and a quiet line counts the time so far against the usual: "4 minutes so far · usually about 10". Past the usual it keeps counting and says nothing worse (C2).

The case for it: no step has to report anything, so every step, the ones that can't be counted included, looks alive the same way. Splash-only work: a sweep sprite moved each frame, a pulse constant, minutes drawn from GLYPHS from the splash's own clock (and a start time kept on disk so the restart after the copy doesn't reset it).

The cost: the motion is the splash's, not the work's. A hub stuck for good sweeps exactly like a hub nearly done, which is the frozen screen with better lighting. And "usually about 10" is the same measured number A needs.

DECIDED 18 NOVEMBER 2026

A, with C's deeper lamp pulse. The steps "getting ready" hid are named as each starts (Unpacking what it came with, Setting up the hub), every step without a quiet line of its own says a first start takes about 10 minutes and happens once, and the lamp pulses 45% to full every 2.4 s until Ready. C's sweep and clock, and B's bar, are not built.

Still owed: "about 10 minutes" is a placeholder until a first start is timed on the NUC and the Pi, and the offline waits inside install.sh are worth cutting whatever this says.

WHICH ONE

Recommendation: A, with C's deeper lamp pulse, now; B's bar on the copy and the download after.

A changes the line on every real step and says up front that a first start takes about 10 minutes and happens once, which answers "is this normal?" before anybody asks. The deeper pulse costs one constant and makes the house read as alive across a room. B is the honest answer for the steps that are really long when they happen (the copy, the download), but it can't help the step that was actually watched, which has nothing to count. C's sweep and clock I would leave out: motion the work doesn't drive is a frozen screen with better lighting.

First, though: measure a first start on the NUC from its log, and cut whatever in install.sh is waiting on a network that isn't there. The fastest first start needs the least reassurance.

Or something else: describe it, and I'll draw it.
